n1: The node’s criterion already distinguishes a frog clearly inside the bowl from one merely on the lid or floor, and the edited image visibly contains a frog inside the bowl. The lone partial trace conflicts with both the other four traces and its own evidence; do not make the criterion more permissive or infer partial completion from the extra frogs. Investigate why equivalent evidence is mapped inconsistently to partial versus complete, and make the status mapping apply the existing placement criterion consistently. The high-confidence repeated variation is a calibration/decision-boundary signal, not evidence that the requested edit is absent. All traces are valid, queried, and dependency-free, so this is not a transport or schema failure.

The node’s criterion already distinguishes complete from partial, but its question asks only whether a frog is inside, which can collapse that distinction and invite inconsistent labels. Align the question with the existing placement criterion: assess whether a frog is visibly within the toilet bowl (not merely on the lid or nearby), and reserve partial for ambiguous or only partly-in placement. In the edited image, one frog appears clearly inside the bowl; others are on the lid and floor, so those extras do not make the requested change partial. The traces mostly call this complete, with one partial trace despite describing the same clear placement and reporting 0.99 confidence. Investigate that criterion/label mapping and trace inconsistency rather than treating the aggregate reference as atomic ground truth. All traces are valid, queried, and dependency-free, so this is not a transport or schema failure.

The node’s criterion already distinguishes clear placement from partial placement, but its question is only binary and may be driving inconsistent status mapping: four traces call the image complete while one calls it partial, despite all describing a frog visibly inside the bowl. Make the decision explicitly apply the supplied rubric and criteria: assess whether at least one frog is visibly within the toilet bowl (not merely on the lid or nearby), then map that evidence consistently to the defined completion status; do not let extra frogs affect fulfillment. The edited image appears to show one frog inside the bowl, another on the lid, and another on the floor, while the source has no frogs. The traces are valid, queried, and dependency-free, so this is not a transport or schema failure. Treat the reference label as an aggregate constraint, not proof that the visible bowl placement is absent or only partial; investigate why the reference says partial versus the repeated high-confidence complete judgments, and avoid forcing either label without resolving the criterion/evidence mismatch.
